description: Mole Negro, the queen of Oaxacan moles, is a majestic dish boasting an incredible depth of flavor from a rich blend of chiles, spices, nuts, and a touch of chocolate. This iconic black mole is a labor of love, resulting in a complex and deeply satisfying sauce that perfectly complements chicken or pork. Prepare to embark on a culinary journey to the heart of Oaxaca with every savory bite.

instructions.title: Prepare and Toast Chiles
instructions.text: Heat a comal or dry skillet over medium heat. Toast the dried chiles in batches for 30 seconds to 1 minute per side, until fragrant but not burnt. Be careful not to burn them, as this will make the mole bitter. Transfer the toasted chiles to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for at least 20 minutes, or until soft. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics and Vegetables
instructions.text: On the same comal, roast the tomatillos, garlic, onion, and tomatoes until softened and slightly charred. This will bring out their natural sweetness and add depth. Set aside. In a separate pan with a tablespoon of lard or oil, fry the plantain slices until golden brown. Drain on paper towels and set aside. Fry the corn tortillas until crispy. Set aside.

instructions.title: Toast Nuts, Seeds, and Spices
instructions.text: In a dry skillet over low heat, toast the almonds, pecans, and sesame seeds until lightly golden and fragrant. Remove and set aside. In the same skillet, toast the anise seeds, cinnamon stick, cloves, and black peppercorns for about 1 minute until aromatic. Add the dried thyme and oregano and toast for another 30 seconds. Be careful not to burn the spices.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Paste
instructions.text: In a blender, combine the rehydrated chiles (reserving some soaking liquid), roasted tomatillos, garlic, onion, tomatoes, fried plantain, fried tortillas, toasted nuts, seeds, and spices. Add about 2 cups of chicken broth and blend until a very smooth paste forms, adding more chile soaking liquid or broth as needed to achieve a thick, pourable consistency. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl to ensure a smooth sauce, pressing on the solids to extract all liquid. Discard any remaining solids.

instructions.title: Simmer the Mole Sauce
instructions.text: Heat the remaining lard or vegetable oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully pour the strained mole paste into the hot oil. It will splatter, so be cautious. Stir constantly for 10-15 minutes, allowing the paste to fry and deepen in color. This step is crucial for developing the mole's rich flavor. Gradually stir in the remaining chicken broth, a cup at a time, bringing the mixture to a gentle simmer after each addition. The sauce should be thick but pourable.

instructions.title: Finish and Serve
instructions.text: Once all the broth is incorporated, reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for at least 1 hour, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The mole should thicken and its flavors will meld beautifully. Stir in the Mexican chocolate until fully melted and incorporated. Add sugar and salt to taste. The mole should have a balance of sweet, savory, and spicy flavors. Add the cooked chicken or turkey to the mole and simmer for another 15-20 minutes to heat through and allow the flavors to marry. Serve hot, garnished with extra sesame seeds, alongside warm tortillas and Mexican rice.

tips: Always toast your chiles and spices carefully; burning them will introduce a bitter flavor to your mole. Work in small batches and watch them closely.
For an even richer flavor, consider using a good quality Mexican chocolate that is specifically made for cooking. It often contains cinnamon and other spices that complement the mole.
Mole Negro improves with age. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat it on the stove over low heat. The flavors will have more time to meld and deepen.
article:
## Unveiling the Soul of Oaxaca: The Irresistible Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)

Imagine a dish so profound, so layered with history and flavor, that it tells the story of an entire region with every spoonful. This is Oaxacan Black Mole, or Mole Negro, a culinary masterpiece from the heart of Mexico. Far more than just a sauce, Mole Negro is a celebration, a ritual, and arguably the most complex and revered of all Mexican dinner recipes. Its deep, smoky, subtly sweet, and intensely savory profile has captivated palates for centuries, making it a bucket-list dish for any food enthusiast. If you've ever dreamt of embarking on a truly authentic Mexican cooking adventure, mastering the Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is an unparalleled journey into the soul of Mexican cuisine.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)?

Oaxacan Black Mole, known locally as Mole Negro, is often considered the "king of moles" due to its intricate preparation and astonishing depth of flavor. Hailing from the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, a region renowned for its seven distinct moles, Mole Negro stands out for its characteristic dark, almost black color and a flavor profile that is nothing short of symphonic. It’s a delicate balance of heat from multiple types of chiles, sweetness from fruits and chocolate, earthiness from nuts and seeds, and a profound savoriness from spices and aromatics.

The creation of Mole Negro is a labor of love, traditionally involving dozens of ingredients meticulously toasted, ground, and slowly simmered. The signature dark hue comes from intensely charred chiles, burnt tortillas, and often dark Mexican chocolate. While the ingredient list can seem daunting, the result is a sauce that is velvety smooth, incredibly rich, and bursting with a complexity that evolves with every bite. It's not just food; it's an edible heritage, a testament to generations of culinary wisdom.

## Ingredients You'll Need for Mole Negro

Preparing an authentic Oaxacan Black Mole recipe requires a dedicated shopping trip and a pantry stocked with specific Mexican staples. Don't be intimidated by the length; each ingredient plays a crucial role in building the mole's incredible character.

**For the Chiles (approx. 15-20 total):**
*   6-8 large Mulato chiles
*   6-8 large Ancho chiles
*   3-4 large Pasilla Oaxaca chiles (smoked pasilla; if unavailable, substitute with more Mulato/Ancho and a chipotle morita for smokiness)
*   1-2 Chilhuacle Negro chiles (highly prized and rare; if unavailable, omit or use another Mulato/Ancho)
*   1-2 Chipotle Morita chiles (for extra smokiness)

**For the Aromatics & Vegetables:**
*   1 large white onion, roughly chopped
*   6-8 cloves garlic, peeled
*   2 ripe Roma tomatoes, halved
*   2 tomatillos, husked and halved
*   1 ripe plantain, sliced
*   ½ cup raisins
*   ¼ cup prunes (pitted)

**For the Nuts & Seeds:**
*   ½ cup raw almonds
*   ¼ cup raw peanuts
*   ¼ cup pumpkin seeds (pepitas)
*   2 tablespoons sesame seeds (plus more for garnish)

**For the Spices:**
*   1 cinnamon stick (about 3 inches)
*   5-6 whole cloves
*   ½ teaspoon whole black peppercorns
*   ½ teaspoon cumin seeds
*   ½ teaspoon coriander seeds
*   ¼ teaspoon anise seeds (optional)

**For the Thickeners & Darkeners:**
*   2 stale corn tortillas, torn
*   1 slice stale bread (bolillo or white bread)
*   1 tablet (90g) authentic Mexican chocolate (e.g., Ibarra or Abuelita)
*   1 small piloncillo cone (Mexican brown sugar) or 2 tablespoons dark brown sugar

**For the Base & Fat:**
*   4-6 cups chicken broth (or vegetable broth for a vegetarian version)
*   ¼ cup lard or vegetable oil
*   Salt to taste

## Step-by-Step Guide to Making Mole Negro

Making this Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is a journey, not a sprint. Take your time, and enjoy the process!

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Remove stems and seeds from all chiles. Lightly toast them in a dry comal or skillet over medium heat for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant but not burnt. Submerge toasted chiles in hot water for 20-30 minutes until softened. Reserve the soaking liquid.
2.  **Toast & Fry Aromatics, Nuts & Spices:** In a large skillet with a little lard/oil, separately toast/fry each group of ingredients until fragrant and lightly browned.
    *   Sauté onion and garlic until softened. Set aside.
    *   Fry plantain slices until golden. Set aside.
    *   Lightly toast almonds, peanuts, pepitas, and sesame seeds separately until fragrant. Set aside.
    *   Lightly toast cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, cumin, coriander, and anise seeds until aromatic. Set aside.
    *   Char the tomatoes and tomatillos directly over a flame or in a dry skillet until blackened. Set aside.
    *   Fry the stale tortillas and bread until crispy. Set aside.
    *   Sauté raisins and prunes briefly until plump. Set aside.
3.  **Blend the Paste:** In batches, combine the rehydrated chiles (reserving soaking liquid), all the toasted/fried ingredients, Mexican chocolate, piloncillo/brown sugar, and about 2 cups of chicken broth. Blend until very smooth. Add a little reserved chile soaking liquid or more broth if needed to aid blending. For the smoothest texture, strain the blended paste through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl. This step is optional but highly recommended.
4.  **Fry the Mole Base:** In a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat ¼ cup of lard or oil over medium heat. Carefully pour the strained mole paste into the hot fat. **This is a crucial step for flavor development and darkening.** Stir constantly with a wooden spoon for at least 20-30 minutes, or until the mole darkens considerably, thickens, and the oil separates from the paste. It will splatter, so use a splatter guard if you have one.
5.  **Simmer and Season:** Gradually add the remaining chicken broth, stirring continuously to incorporate it into the thick paste. Bring the mole to a gentle simmer. Reduce heat to low, cover partially, and cook for at least 1-2 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The longer it simmers, the more the flavors will meld and deepen. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt as needed. The mole should be thick but pourable; add more broth if it’s too thick.

## Pro Tips for the Best Oaxacan Black Mole

*   **Quality Chiles are Key:** The foundation of a great mole is fresh, high-quality dried chiles. Seek out specialty Mexican markets.
*   **Don't Rush the Toasting:** Each ingredient needs its specific level of toasting or frying to release its full flavor. Pay attention to each item.
*   **Balance is Everything:** Taste frequently! Mole Negro is about a harmonious balance of sweet, spicy, smoky, and savory. Adjust with more salt, piloncillo, or even a tiny splash of vinegar at the end if it needs brightness.
*   **Patience is a Virtue:** This is not a quick meal. The long simmering time allows the complex flavors to meld and mature.
*   **Embrace the Strainer:** While optional, straining the blended paste through a fine-mesh sieve creates an incredibly smooth, luxurious texture that is characteristic of authentic Mole Negro.
*   **Resting Improves Flavor:** Like many complex sauces, mole often tastes even better the day after it's made, as the flavors continue to develop.

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

The traditional way to enjoy this Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is with poultry.
*   **Chicken or Turkey:** Simmer cooked chicken or turkey pieces directly in the mole sauce until heated through.
*   **Enchiladas:** Use the mole to coat enchiladas filled with cheese, chicken, or vegetables.
*   **Over Rice:** Serve a generous ladle of mole over white rice, accompanied by your protein of choice.
*   **Tamales:** A rich filling for tamales.
*   **Tacos:** A decadent sauce for soft tacos with shredded meat.
*   **Vegetarian Options:** Serve with roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or cauliflower steaks.
*   **Garnish:** Always finish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds, and sometimes finely diced white onion and cilantro for freshness.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the traditional Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is a masterpiece, you can make minor adjustments based on availability or dietary needs.

*   **Chiles:** If Chilhuacle Negro or Pasilla Oaxaca are impossible to find, increase the amounts of Mulato and Ancho chiles. For smokiness, a chipotle morita is a good addition.
*   **Nuts/Seeds:** Feel free to adjust the ratio of nuts and seeds based on what you have or prefer. Walnuts or pecans can be added.
*   **Sweeteners:** Dark brown sugar can replace piloncillo. For a richer chocolate flavor, you can add a small amount of unsweetened cocoa powder along with the Mexican chocolate.
*   **Vegetarian Mole:** Use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth. Serve with hearty vegetables like roasted squash, plant-based proteins, or black beans.
*   **Spice Level:** To control heat, remove more seeds from the chiles before rehydrating.

## Storage and Reheating Tips

One of the great joys of making a large batch of Oaxacan Black Mole is that it stores wonderfully, allowing you to savor your efforts for days or even months.

*   **Refrigeration:** Store leftover mole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5-7 days.
*   **Freezing:** Mole freezes exceptionally well. Portion it into freezer-safe containers or bags and freeze for up to 3-6 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.
*   **Reheating:** Gently reheat the mole on the stovetop over low heat, stirring frequently. If it has thickened too much, add a splash of chicken or vegetable broth or water until it reaches your desired consistency. Avoid boiling rapidly, as this can dull the flavors.

Embarking on the creation of Mole Negro is a culinary adventure that rewards patience and passion with an unforgettable gastronomic experience. This Oaxacan Black Mole recipe isn't just about cooking; it's about connecting with a rich cultural heritage and bringing a truly extraordinary Mexican dinner recipe to your table. So, gather your ingredients, clear your schedule, and prepare to make magic in your kitchen.
